subject: chemistry-1
question: Carbon dioxide contains two strongly polar C=O bonds, yet the whole molecule is nonpolar. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: The molecule is linear, so two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
The individual C=O bond dipoles are too small to give the molecule measurable polarity.
Double bonds share four electrons, and that larger shared count cancels bond polarity.
Lone pairs on the central carbon atom offset the partial charges on the two oxygens.

explanation:
Molecular polarity is the vector sum of bond dipoles, so geometry matters as much as electronegativity. Each C=O bond is genuinely polar, with an electronegativity difference of 3.44 - 2.55 = 0.89, but the central carbon has no lone pairs, giving a linear 180-degree arrangement in which two identical dipoles point directly away from each other and sum to zero. Water contains comparably polar O-H bonds but is bent at about 104.5 degrees, so its bond dipoles cannot cancel and the molecule has a net dipole of 1.85 D.

ELI-10: Think of the two oxygens as equally strong pulls on the electrons, aimed in exactly opposite directions along a straight line. Real forces exist on each bond, but they add up to nothing overall, so the molecule has no plus end or minus end for a neighbor to grab. The key skill is checking geometry before declaring a molecule polar: identical polar bonds arranged symmetrically cancel, and the same bonds arranged asymmetrically, as in bent water, do not.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
